prompt: Why not write 'Language: Portuguese' into each article's text before embedding, instead of storing a language field?
hint: Is 'is this in Portuguese' a matter of degree?

choices.text: Because a longer text takes more tokens to embed
choices.why: A few words cost almost nothing. The problem is what a similarity score can and cannot answer.

choices.text: Because the model would refuse the extra words
choices.why: A model embeds any text it is given. It would embed the label and blend it into the meaning.

choices.text: It is a yes-or-no question; similarity gives degrees
choices.why: Right. A label in the text nudges a vector; a field tested by a filter answers exactly, every time.

choices.text: Because Portuguese articles have no vectors in an English model
choices.why: They have vectors, 384 numbers like any text; lesson 1 showed they land as noise to an English model, which is one more reason a label would not help.

prompt: By the counts `jq` printed, how many of the help centre's articles are NOT in the payments category?
hint: All the articles, minus the payments ones.

prompt: Match each metadata field to the question it answers for a search.
hint: One question belongs to the vector, not to any field.

pairs.right: Are they allowed to see it?

right_distractors: Is it about the same subject as the question?

prompt: 'I was charged twice' with the filter category = 'payments' and k = 3: the post-filter returned 2 articles. Why not 3?
hint: Look at what the three nearest were.

choices.text: The payments category has only two articles
choices.why: It has six, and the pre-filter found a third, h25.

choices.text: A returns article filled one of the 3
choices.why: Right. The filter ran on the 3 already picked and dropped one; post-filtering never goes back for more.

choices.text: The third payments article scored below zero
choices.why: h25 scored 0.112, above zero. A score is not what removed it; it was never among the first three.

choices.text: k counts the filtered-out article as one of the 3
choices.why: k picked three articles; the filter then removed one. Nothing counts it, it is simply gone.

prompt: In `ten.sql`, every query asked pgvector for 10 Portuguese rows and got 0 or 1. What produced that?
hint: Read where the Filter line sits in the plan.

choices.text: The table had fewer than 10 Portuguese rows
choices.why: One row in 50 of 5,000 is 100 Portuguese rows, and the partial index later returned 10 for every query.

choices.text: The planner ignored the WHERE clause
choices.why: The plan shows the Filter line, and every row returned was Portuguese. The WHERE ran, just after the index.

choices.text: The index yielded its 40 nearest candidates and the filter kept the Portuguese ones
choices.why: Right. ef_search caps the candidates at 40, and one in fifty of them is Portuguese: less than one on average.

choices.text: Random vectors cannot be filtered by language
choices.why: The language is an ordinary column; the vectors being random changes nothing about how WHERE works.

prompt: pgvector's HNSW scan yields 40 candidates and one row in 50 is Portuguese. On average, how many Portuguese rows survive the filter?
hint: 40 times the share that passes.

prompt: Running the search, keeping its k nearest and only then dropping the ones that fail the condition is called ___.
hint: The filter comes after.

prompt: With hnsw.ef_search at 400, query row 7 still got only 3 of its 10 Portuguese rows. What follows for a page that must show 10?
hint: Was 400 a guarantee for the other rows, or a better chance?

choices.text: Raise it to 1,000 and the problem is gone
choices.why: A wider list makes a shortfall rarer. Nothing in it promises that the walk meets 10 Portuguese rows.

choices.text: Move the filter elsewhere
choices.why: Right. A pre-filter, a partial index or a filter applied during the walk returns 10 whenever 10 pass; ef_search only improves the odds.

choices.text: Row 7 has fewer than 10 Portuguese neighbours
choices.why: Every row has the same 100 Portuguese rows to choose from; the partial index returned 10 for row 7.

choices.text: The index is broken and has to be rebuilt
choices.why: Nothing is broken. An approximate walk visits part of the graph, and on that part only 3 passed.

prompt: Put in order what happens in pgvector 0.6.0 to a query with WHERE lang = 'pt' that the planner sends through the HNSW index.
hint: The filter is not first.
items: The index walks its graph from the entry point
It yields up to ef_search candidates, nearest first
PostgreSQL tests lang on each candidate
LIMIT keeps at most 10 that passed
The query returns what is left, maybe fewer than 10
trap: The language test does not come before the walk: that would be a pre-filter, which is what the partial index did.

prompt: `prefilter_cost.py` took 0.7 ms for lang = 'pt' and 83.3 ms for lang = 'en'. Why the difference?
hint: Count the rows each one searched.

choices.text: English text takes longer to compare than Portuguese
choices.why: These are random vectors with a label. The arithmetic per row is the same whatever the label says.

choices.text: The English query had to sort all 10 results
choices.why: Both sorted 10. The difference is in how many rows were scored before that.

choices.text: The first run was cold, and English ran later
choices.why: Each time is the best of 20 runs, so a cold start is not in it.

choices.text: It searched 178,000 rows exactly instead of 2,000
choices.why: Right. A pre-filter is an exact search over what passes, and its cost follows the size of that subset.

prompt: How many times longer did the pre-filtered query take for lang = 'en' than for lang = 'pt'? Round to a whole number.
hint: 83.3 ms against 0.7 ms.

prompt: After the partial index `WHERE lang = 'pt'` was built, what did `ten.sql` return?
hint: Which queries can use an index built with that condition?

choices.text: 10 Portuguese rows for every query, and the Spanish column unchanged
choices.why: Right. Every row in the partial index already passes, so the Portuguese query has nothing to filter out; the Spanish one still goes through the full index and its filter.

choices.text: 10 rows in both columns
choices.why: The Spanish counts stayed between 2 and 6. The new index covers lang = 'pt' and nothing else.

choices.text: The same counts as before, since the planner kept the old index
choices.why: The Portuguese column went from 0 or 1 to 10 in every row, so the planner did use the new index.

choices.text: An error, since a table may have only one HNSW index
choices.why: CREATE INDEX printed CREATE INDEX, and the table then had two HNSW indexes.

prompt: A table stores documents for 20,000 customers, filtered by customer_id. Someone proposes one partial HNSW index per customer. What is wrong with that?
hint: A partial index exists for each value you give it.

choices.text: Partial indexes cannot use a vector operator
choices.why: The lesson built one with vector_cosine_ops and the planner used it.

choices.text: Twenty thousand indexes to build and maintain
choices.why: Right. A partial index suits a field with a few values that matter; a value per customer wants the other designs in the tenants section.

choices.text: A partial index returns fewer than k rows, like a post-filter
choices.why: The opposite: every row in it passes, so it returned 10 of 10 in ten.sql.

choices.text: It would leak documents between customers
choices.why: Each index covers only its own customer's rows. The cost is the number of indexes, not a leak.

prompt: In `lance_filter.py`, `prefilter=False` returned an empty list. Why?
hint: What were the 3 nearest articles to the English question?

choices.text: LanceDB cannot filter on a text column
choices.why: With prefilter=True the same filter on the same column returned three articles.

choices.text: The table had no index, so filtering was switched off
choices.why: There was no vector index, and the search ran exactly; the filter ran too, after it.

choices.text: It filtered the 3 nearest, all of them English
choices.why: Right. That is post-filtering: the same empty list post_filter gave in filtered.py.

choices.text: The cosine metric ranks Portuguese articles last
choices.why: The metric does not look at languages. The three Portuguese rows were simply not among the three nearest.

prompt: Qdrant in local mode warned that payload indexes have no effect. What does that tell you about the filtered query it then ran?
hint: How does local mode search?

choices.text: The filter was ignored, so the results are unfiltered
choices.why: The results were h40, h39 and h38, the three Portuguese articles. The filter ran; the index for it was what went unused.

choices.text: The query fell back to a post-filter and lost results
choices.why: It returned all three Portuguese articles with k = 3, which a post-filter on this question does not.

choices.text: It scored every point and masked out those failing the filter, exactly
choices.why: Right. Local mode is exact and needs no index for the filter; the payload index matters to the server's HNSW graph.

choices.text: The collection has to be created again with the index in place
choices.why: Recreating it changes nothing in local mode. The warning says to use the server if you need payload indexes.

prompt: In LanceDB, `.where("lang = 'pt'", ___=True)` applies the condition before the vector search.
hint: The parameter's name says when.

prompt: Which of these returned the three Portuguese articles for 'how do I return a book' with the language filter and k = 3? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them filter after the three nearest are picked.

choices.text: Chroma with where
choices.why: Yes: h40, h39 and h38, the condition deciding which records could be returned.

choices.text: LanceDB with prefilter=False
choices.why: It returned an empty list: the three nearest were English.

choices.text: Qdrant local with a Filter
choices.why: Yes: it scores every point and masks out the rest.

choices.text: pre_filter in store.py
choices.why: Yes: it searched only the three Portuguese rows.

choices.text: post_filter in store.py
choices.why: It returned []: the filter came after the three English articles.

prompt: By Qdrant's documentation of filterable HNSW, why does a narrow filter not leave its server short of results the way it left pgvector 0.6.0?
hint: Where does the condition get checked?

choices.text: Its default candidate list is far larger than 40
choices.why: A larger list would only make a shortfall rarer, as ef_search 400 did. The difference is where the condition is checked.

choices.text: It checks the condition during the walk, or searches a small subset exactly
choices.why: Right. Rejected points do not use up the result list, and a narrow filter is served by an exact search over the few points that pass.

choices.text: It keeps a separate collection for each payload value
choices.why: That is the one-collection-per-tenant design, which you choose yourself. Filterable HNSW works inside one collection.

choices.text: It returns fewer results too, and pads them with unfiltered ones
choices.why: Padding with rows that fail the filter would break the filter's meaning. Nothing in the lesson describes it.

prompt: `tenant_search.py` with no shop named failed with an error. Why is that the behaviour you want?
hint: Compare it with what an empty filter does in most code.

choices.text: Errors are cheaper than empty result sets
choices.why: Cost is not the point. What matters is what a forgotten tenant gets to see.

choices.text: A connection that names no shop gets nothing
choices.why: Right. The policy compares each row with app.shop, and with no app.shop the query cannot run, so a forgotten setting fails instead of leaking.

choices.text: It shows the helpdesk role has no SELECT permission
choices.why: helpdesk has SELECT; the same role returned rows as soon as a shop was set.

choices.text: The table has no rows for a missing shop, so PostgreSQL reports it
choices.why: PostgreSQL reported an unknown setting, not a missing shop. A query that finds no rows returns an empty result, not an error.

prompt: Marginalia's API accepts `{"query": ..., "shop": ...}` in the request body and passes `shop` to the vector search as a filter. What is the flaw?
hint: Who decides the value of shop?

choices.text: A JSON body is slower to parse than a query string
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; any channel the client fills has the same flaw.

choices.text: The filter should be applied before the search
choices.why: Pre- or post-, a filter whose value the client chooses filters for whatever the client asks.

choices.text: Vector databases cannot filter on a text field like shop
choices.why: All four engines in this lesson filtered on text fields such as lang.

choices.text: The shop is chosen by the client, so any shop is open
choices.why: Right. The tenant has to come from the signed-in session on the server; a value in the request is a claim.

prompt: Why does `tenant_search.py` switch to the role helpdesk instead of searching as ana?
hint: Who does row-level security apply to?

choices.text: Owners and superusers skip RLS
choices.why: Right. As ana the search would see every shop's rows; the policy binds a role that is neither owner nor superuser.

choices.text: ana cannot read the vector type
choices.why: ana created the extension and loaded the table with vectors in shops.py.

choices.text: helpdesk is faster because it has fewer permissions
choices.why: Permissions do not change the speed of a query. They change which rows the policy lets through.

choices.text: app.shop can be set only by a role named helpdesk
choices.why: Any role can set a custom setting; it is the policy, not the setting, that needs a role it applies to.

prompt: PostgreSQL's ___ security adds a policy's condition to every query on a table.
hint: It works per row.

prompt: Match each search that ran in this lesson to how its filter was applied.
hint: One description matches none of them.

pairs.right: The condition chose which records could be returned
Every point scored, the filter applied as a mask

pairs.left: pgvector through the full HNSW index
pairs.right: Each candidate the index yielded was tested

right_distractors: The filter was handed to a reranker

prompt: Order these pre-filtered queries from `prefilter_cost.py` from fastest to slowest.
hint: The time follows the rows searched.
trap: The narrowest filter is the fastest, not the slowest: a pre-filter does less work the more the filter removes.

prompt: A shop shows 'books like this one, in stock' with k = 10 over an HNSW index, and 95% of its books are in stock. Which way of filtering fits?
hint: Apply this lesson's rule about filter width.

choices.text: An exact pre-filter, since only it is correct
choices.why: It is correct and searches 95% of the books by brute force for every page view, which is the wide-filter case where pre-filtering is slow.

choices.text: Search, then filter
choices.why: Right. With 95% passing, a post-filter over the candidates loses about one in twenty, and widening the candidate list a little covers it.

choices.text: A partial index for each book
choices.why: A partial index is per value of a condition, not per book; one per book would be thousands of tiny indexes.

choices.text: Row-level security on the stock column
choices.why: Stock is not a permission. Row-level security is for who may see a row, and here everyone may.
